Precocious

prih-KOH-shus — rhymes with ferocious · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Precocious describes a child who shows abilities, skills, or maturity well beyond what is typical for their age.

The precocious six-year-old corrected the museum guide's dinosaur facts.

Worked Example

The precocious eight-year-old had already read calculus textbooks and was inventing her own mathematical proofs.

Precocious specifically emphasizes that the child's abilities are far beyond what's normal or expected for her age — she's developmentally advanced, not just smart. It's more precise than 'gifted' or 'smart' because it highlights the unusual earliness of her maturity and skills.

How Precocious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

gifted

gifted: having unusual natural talent or ability

mature

mature: acting older than one's actual age

advanced

advanced: further along than others the same age

Antonyms

delayed

delayed: developing later than is typical

immature

immature: less developed than expected for one's age

How Strong Is It? — delayed → age-appropriate → advanced → precocious

delayed vs. precocious

delayed vs. precocious: Delayed sits at the opposite end of the scale from precocious: a delayed child develops later than is typical, while a precocious child develops strikingly earlier than expected.

age-appropriate vs. precocious

age-appropriate vs. precocious: Age-appropriate is the neutral middle, well below precocious — age-appropriate abilities match what is normal for a child's age, while precocious abilities leap far beyond it.

advanced vs. precocious

advanced vs. precocious: Advanced is strong but still weaker than precocious: an advanced student is somewhat ahead of peers, while a precocious one shows abilities dramatically beyond their years.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — pre-

Prefix — pre-: before (Latin prae-) (Latin)

Root — -coc-

Root — -coc-: to cook, to ripen (Latin coquere) (Latin)

Suffix — -ious

Suffix — -ious: full of, characterized by (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin praecox described fruit that 'cooked' — that is, ripened — before its usual time. A precocious child is exactly that: 'ripened early,' showing abilities and maturity well before the typical age.

Use the root in a new word: concoct

Use the root in a new word: concoct: When you concoct a stew, you 'cook' ingredients together — the same Latin root coquere, 'to cook or ripen,' hides inside precocious, which literally means 'ripened early.'

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / formal

Precocious is the precise word when you want to emphasize that a child's abilities or maturity are far beyond their age. In casual conversation, 'smart' or 'mature for their age' works fine.
